text:
Washington won 5-3, but the model scores it as a coin flip: each team finished with about four expected goals, and each wins half of the simulated replays. The Capitals made the early minutes count. Anthony Beauvillier scored 23 seconds in, Bryan Rust answered for Pittsburgh a minute later, and Tom Wilson put Washington back in front midway through the period. In those first 20 minutes the Capitals generated 2.41 expected goals to Pittsburgh's 0.24, a lopsided stretch that produced a 2-1 lead.

The second period belonged to Pittsburgh in terms of chances (2.11 expected goals to 0.99), though Washington got the goals that settled things. Pierre-Luc Dubois scored off a Wilson pass, and Alex Tuch made it 4-1 on a 33 percent chance, with Wilson again credited with the assist. Pittsburgh's reply came quickly. Tommy Novak scored 51 seconds later on a 37 percent look, and Nick Robertson tipped in a third with 1:59 left in the period to make it 4-3. Novak's individual expected goals (1.06) say he was in the right spots all night, and he finished with one.

Ryan Leonard's power-play goal early in the third restored a two-goal margin, and Pittsburgh never got closer despite another 1.62 expected goals to Washington's 0.59 in the period. Wilson's two assists and a goal earned him first star. Logan Thompson saved about one goal more than expected, while Arturs Silovs let in one more than the shots called for. That one-goal gap between the goalies is a fair summary of the night: two teams played to a draw on chances, and one goaltender gave back just enough to decide it.
